**Alfred the Great** ([Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_language "Old English language"): _**Ælfrǣd**_[[ˈæɫvˌræːd]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Old_English "Help:IPA/Old English"); c.849 – 26 October 899) was [King of the West Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_West_Saxons "King of the West Saxons") from 871 to 886, and [King of the Anglo-Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Anglo-Saxons "King of the Anglo-Saxons") from 886 until his death in 899. He was the youngest son of King [Æthelwulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwulf "Æthelwulf") and Æthelwulf's first wife [Osburh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osburh "Osburh"), who both died when Alfred was young. Three of Alfred's brothers, [Æthelbald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelbald,_King_of_Wessex "Æthelbald, King of Wessex"), [Æthelberht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht,_King_of_Wessex "Æthelberht, King of Wessex") and [Æthelred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelred_I_of_Wessex "Æthelred I of Wessex"), reigned in turn before him. Under Alfred's rule, considerable administrative and military reforms were introduced, prompting lasting change in England.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolyneaux2015[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_September_2022]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears. (September_2022)%22%3Epage needed%3C/span%3E]]%3C/i%3E]%3C/sup%3E-3)

After ascending the throne, Alfred spent several years fighting [Viking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking "Viking") invasions. He won a decisive victory at the [Battle of Edington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edington "Battle of Edington") in 878 and made an agreement with the Vikings, dividing England between [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") territory and the Viking-ruled [Danelaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danelaw "Danelaw"), which consisted of [Scandinavian York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_York "Scandinavian York"), the north-east [Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands "Midlands"), and [East Anglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Anglia "East Anglia"). Alfred also oversaw the conversion of the Viking leader [Guthrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guthrum "Guthrum") to Christianity. He defended his kingdom against the Viking attempt at conquest, becoming the dominant ruler in England.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke200127%E2%80%9328-4) In 886 Alfred began styling himself "King of the Anglo-Saxons" after reoccupying [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_London "Anglo-Saxon London") from the Vikings. Details of his life are described in a work by the 9th-century Welsh scholar and bishop [Asser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asser "Asser").

Alfred had a reputation as a learned and merciful man of a gracious and level-headed nature who encouraged education, establishing a court school for both nobles and commoners to be educated in both English and Latin, and improving the legal system and military structure and his people's quality of life. He was given the epithet "the Great" from as early as the 13th century, though it was only popularised from the 16th century.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirth2024-5) Alfred is the only native-born English monarch to be labelled as such.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Britain_886.jpg/500px-Britain_886.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Britain_886.jpg)

Map of Britain in 886

Alfred's grandfather [Ecgberht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecgberht,_King_of_Wessex "Ecgberht, King of Wessex") became King of Wessex in 802, and in the view of the historian [Richard Abels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Abels "Richard Abels"), it must have seemed very unlikely to contemporaries that he would establish a lasting dynasty. For 200 years, three families had fought for the West Saxon throne, and no son had followed his father as king. No ancestor of Ecgberht had been a king of Wessex since [Ceawlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceawlin "Ceawlin") in the late sixth century, but he was believed to be a paternal descendant of [Cerdic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerdic "Cerdic"), the founder of the [West Saxon dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_Wessex "List of monarchs of Wessex").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-8) This made Ecgberht an [ætheling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86theling "Ætheling") – a prince eligible for the throne. But after Ecgberht's reign, descent from Cerdic was no longer sufficient to make a man an ætheling. When Ecgberht died in 839, he was succeeded by his son Æthelwulf; all subsequent West Saxon kings were descendants of Ecgberht and Æthelwulf, and were also sons of kings.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels200284%E2%80%9385Dumville197917%E2%80%9318Yorke1990142%E2%80%93143,_148%E2%80%93149-9)

At the beginning of the ninth century, England was almost wholly under the control of the [Anglo-Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon "Anglo-Saxon"). Mercia dominated southern England, but its supremacy came to an end in 825 when it was decisively defeated by Ecgberht at the [Battle of Ellendun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ellendun "Battle of Ellendun").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynes199528,_39%E2%80%9341-10) Mercia and Wessex became allies, which was important in the resistance to [Viking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking "Viking") attacks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199828%E2%80%9329-11) In 853, King Burgred of Mercia requested West Saxon help to suppress a Welsh rebellion, and Æthelwulf led a West Saxon contingent in a successful joint campaign. The same year, Burgred married Æthelwulf's daughter, Æthelswith.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKirby2000161-12)

In 825, Ecgberht sent Æthelwulf to invade the Mercian sub-kingdom of [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kent "Kingdom of Kent"), and its sub-king, [Baldred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldred_of_Kent "Baldred of Kent"), was driven out shortly afterwards. By 830, [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Essex "Kingdom of Essex"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey") and [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sussex "Kingdom of Sussex") had submitted to Ecgberht, and he had appointed Æthelwulf to rule the south-eastern territories as king of Kent.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynes1993120%E2%80%93121Kirby2000155%E2%80%93156-13) The Vikings ravaged the [Isle of Sheppey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Sheppey "Isle of Sheppey") in 835, and the following year they defeated Ecgberht at [Carhampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhampton "Carhampton") in Somerset,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards2004Kirby2000171-14) but in 838 he was victorious over an alliance of [Cornishmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornishmen "Cornishmen") and Vikings at the [Battle of Hingston Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hingston_Down "Battle of Hingston Down"), reducing Cornwall to the status of a [client kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Client_kingdom "Client kingdom").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTECharles-Edwards2013431-15) When Æthelwulf succeeded to the throne, he appointed his eldest son Æthelstan as sub-king of Kent.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2004-16) Ecgberht and Æthelwulf may not have intended a permanent union between Wessex and Kent because they both appointed sons as sub-kings, and charters in Wessex were attested (witnessed) by West Saxon magnates, while Kentish charters were witnessed by the Kentish elite; both kings kept overall control, and the sub-kings were not allowed to issue their own coinage.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199831-17)

Viking raids increased in the early 840s on both sides of the English Channel, and in 843 Æthelwulf was defeated at Carhampton.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2004-16) In 850, Æthelstan defeated a Danish fleet off [Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwich,_Kent "Sandwich, Kent") in the first recorded naval battle in English history.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStenton1971244-18) In 851, Æthelwulf and his second son, Æthelbald, defeated the Vikings at the [Battle of Aclea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aclea "Battle of Aclea") and, according to the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_, "there made the greatest slaughter of a heathen raiding-army that we have heard tell of up to this present day, and there took the victory".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwanton200064-19) Æthelwulf died in 858 and was succeeded by his oldest surviving son, Æthelbald, as king of Wessex and by his next oldest son, Æthelberht, as king of Kent. Æthelbald only survived his father by two years, and Æthelberht then for the first time united Wessex and Kent into a single kingdom.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199889%E2%80%9394-20)

## Childhood

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Childhood")]

Further information: [House of Wessex family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wessex_family_tree "House of Wessex family tree")

Alfred was the youngest son of [Æthelwulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwulf "Æthelwulf"), king of [Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wessex "Wessex"), and his wife [Osburh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osburh "Osburh").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199826-21) According to his biographer, [Asser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asser "Asser"), writing in 893, "In the year of our Lord's Incarnation 849 Alfred, King of the Anglo-Saxons", was born at the royal estate called [Wantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wantage "Wantage"), in the district known as [Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire "Berkshire")[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-wantage1-2) ("which is so called from Berroc Wood, where the box tree grows very abundantly"). This date has been accepted by the editors of Asser's biography, [Simon Keynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Keynes "Simon Keynes") and [Michael Lapidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lapidge "Michael Lapidge"),[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198313,_67,_101-22) and by other historians such as [David Dumville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Dumville "David Dumville"), [Justin Pollard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Pollard "Justin Pollard") and Richard Huscroft.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDumville199623Huscroft2019xii-23) West Saxon genealogical lists state that Alfred was 23 when he became king in April 871, implying that he was born between April 847 and April 848.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwanton20004Dumville198625-24) This dating is adopted in the biography of Alfred by [Alfred Smyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_P._Smyth "Alfred P. Smyth"), who regards Asser's biography as fraudulent,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmyth19953-25) an allegation which is rejected by other historians.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2006Keynes201451-26)[Richard Abels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Abels "Richard Abels") in his biography discusses both sources but does not decide between them and dates Alfred's birth as 847–49,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199845%E2%80%9346-27) while [Patrick Wormald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Wormald "Patrick Wormald") in his _[Oxford Dictionary of National Biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford\_Dictionary\_of\_National\_Biography "Oxford Dictionary of National Biography")_ article dates it 848–49.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2006-28) Berkshire had been historically disputed between Wessex and the midland kingdom of [Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia "Mercia"), and as late as 844, a charter showed that it was part of Mercia, but Alfred's birth in the county is evidence that, by the late 840s, control had passed to Wessex.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199826,_45%E2%80%9346Wormald2006-29)

He was the youngest of six children. His eldest brother, [Æthelstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelstan_of_Kent "Æthelstan of Kent"), was old enough to be appointed sub-king of Kent in 839, almost 10 years before Alfred was born. He died in the early 850s. Alfred's next three brothers were successively kings of Wessex. [Æthelbald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelbald,_King_of_Wessex "Æthelbald, King of Wessex") (858–860) and [Æthelberht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht,_King_of_Wessex "Æthelberht, King of Wessex") (860–865) were also much older than Alfred, but [Æthelred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelred_I,_King_of_Wessex "Æthelred I, King of Wessex") (865–871) was only a year or two older. Alfred's only known sister, [Æthelswith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelswith "Æthelswith"), married [Burgred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgred_of_Mercia "Burgred of Mercia"), King of Mercia in 853. Most historians think that Osburh was the mother of all Æthelwulf's children, but some suggest that the older ones were born to an unrecorded first wife. Osburh was descended from the rulers of the [Isle of Wight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight "Isle of Wight"). She was described by Asser as "a most religious woman, noble in character and noble by birth".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198368-30) She had died by 856 when Æthelwulf married [Judith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_of_Flanders "Judith of Flanders"), daughter of [Charles the Bald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_the_Bald "Charles the Bald"), King of [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia "West Francia").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199845%E2%80%9350,_55Nelson2003295Wormald2006Miller2004-31)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/%C3%86thelwulf_-_MS_Royal_14_B_VI.jpg/250px-%C3%86thelwulf_-_MS_Royal_14_B_VI.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%C3%86thelwulf_-_MS_Royal_14_B_VI.jpg)

Alfred's father [Æthelwulf of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwulf_of_Wessex "Æthelwulf of Wessex") in the early 14th-century _Genealogical Roll of the Kings of England_

According to Asser, in his childhood Alfred won a beautifully decorated book of English poetry, offered as a prize by his mother to the first of her sons able to memorise it. He must have had it read to him because his mother died when he was about six and he did not learn to read until he was 12.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard200654%E2%80%9355-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199855%E2%80%9356-33) In 853 Alfred is reported by the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_ to have been sent to Rome, where he was [confirmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmed "Confirmed") by [Pope Leo IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_IV "Pope Leo IV"), who "anointed him as king".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilesIngram1996Year_853-34)[Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") writers later interpreted this as an anticipatory coronation in preparation for his eventual succession to the throne of Wessex. This is unlikely; his succession could not have been foreseen at the time because Alfred had three living elder brothers. A letter of Leo IV shows that Alfred was made a "consul" and a misinterpretation of this investiture, deliberate or accidental, could explain later confusion.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard200663-35)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2006-28) It may be based upon the fact that Alfred later accompanied his father on a pilgrimage to Rome where he spent some time at the court of Charles the Bald around 854–55.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels199855-36) On their return from Rome in 856, Æthelwulf was deposed by his son [Æthelbald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelbald_of_Wessex "Æthelbald of Wessex"). With civil war looming, the magnates of the realm met in council to form a compromise. Æthelbald retained the western shires (i.e. historical Wessex), and Æthelwulf ruled in the east, possibly as King of Kent. After Æthelwulf died in 858, Wessex was ruled by three of Alfred's brothers in succession: Æthelbald, [Æthelberht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht_of_Wessex "Æthelberht of Wessex") and [Æthelred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelred_of_Wessex "Æthelred of Wessex").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrofton20068-37)

## The reigns of Alfred's brothers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The reigns of Alfred's brothers")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/England_Great_Army_map.svg/250px-England_Great_Army_map.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:England_Great_Army_map.svg)

A map of the route taken by the Viking [Great Heathen Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Heathen_Army "Great Heathen Army") which arrived in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") from [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") and [southern Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Sweden "Southern Sweden") in 865.

Alfred is not mentioned during the short reigns of his older brothers Æthelbald and Æthelberht. The _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_ describes the [Great Heathen Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Heathen_Army "Great Heathen Army") of Danes landing in East Anglia with the intent of conquering the four kingdoms which constituted Anglo-Saxon England in 865.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198316%E2%80%9317-38) Alfred's public life began in 865 at age 16 with the accession of his third brother, 18-year-old Æthelred. During this period, Bishop Asser gave Alfred the unique title of _secundarius_, which may indicate a position similar to the Celtic [tanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanist "Tanist"), a recognised successor closely associated with the reigning monarch. This arrangement may have been sanctioned by Alfred's father or by the [Witan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witan "Witan") to guard against the danger of a disputed succession should Æthelred fall in battle. It was a well known tradition among other Germanic peoples – such as the Swedes and Franks to whom the Anglo-Saxons were closely related – to crown a successor as royal prince and military commander.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39)

### Viking invasion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Viking invasion")]

In 868 Alfred was recorded as fighting beside Æthelred in a failed attempt to keep the Great Heathen Army led by [Ivar the Boneless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivar_the_Boneless "Ivar the Boneless") out of the adjoining [Kingdom of Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Mercia "Kingdom of Mercia").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilesIngram1996Year_868-40) The Danes arrived in his homeland at the end of 870, and nine engagements were fought in the following year, with mixed results; the places and dates of two of these battles have not been recorded. A successful skirmish at the [Battle of Englefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Englefield "Battle of Englefield") in Berkshire on 31 December 870 was followed by a severe defeat at the siege and the [Battle of Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Reading_(871) "Battle of Reading (871)") by Ivar's brother [Halfdan Ragnarsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfdan_Ragnarsson "Halfdan Ragnarsson") on 5 January 871. Four days later, the Anglo-Saxons won a victory at the [Battle of Ashdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ashdown "Battle of Ashdown") on the [Berkshire Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Wessex_Downs_AONB "North Wessex Downs AONB"), possibly near [Compton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton,_Berkshire "Compton, Berkshire") or [Aldworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldworth "Aldworth").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39) The Saxons were defeated at the [Battle of Basing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Basing "Battle of Basing") on 22 January. They were defeated again on 22 March at the [Battle of Merton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Merton "Battle of Merton") (perhaps Marden in Wiltshire or Martin in Dorset).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39) Æthelred died shortly afterwards in April 871.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39)

## King at war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: King at war")]

### Early struggles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Early struggles")]

In April 871, King Æthelred died and Alfred acceded to the throne of Wessex and the burden of its defence, even though Æthelred left two under-age sons, [Æthelhelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelhelm "Æthelhelm") and [Æthelwold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwold_of_Wessex "Æthelwold of Wessex"). This was in accordance with the agreement that Æthelred and Alfred had made earlier that year in an assembly at an unidentified place called Swinbeorg. The brothers had agreed that whichever of them outlived the other would inherit the personal property that King Æthelwulf had left jointly to his sons in his will. The deceased's sons would receive only whatever property and riches their father had settled upon them and whatever additional lands their uncle had acquired. The unstated premise was that the surviving brother would be king. Given the Danish invasion and the youth of his nephews, Alfred's accession probably went uncontested.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998135-41)

While he was busy with the burial ceremonies for his brother, the Danes defeated the Saxon army in his absence at an unnamed spot and then again in his presence at [Wilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilton,_Wiltshire "Wilton, Wiltshire") in May.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39) The defeat at Wilton smashed any remaining hope that Alfred could drive the invaders from his kingdom. Alfred was forced instead to make peace with them. Although the terms of the peace are not recorded, Bishop Asser wrote that the pagans agreed to vacate the realm and made good their promise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998140%E2%80%93141-42)

The Viking army withdrew from Reading in the autumn of 871 to take up winter quarters in Mercian [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_London "Anglo-Saxon London"). Although not mentioned by Asser or by the _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_, Alfred probably paid the Vikings silver to leave, much as the Mercians were to do in the following year.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998140%E2%80%93141-42)[Hoards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoard "Hoard") dating to the Viking occupation of London in 871/872 have been excavated at [Croydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croydon "Croydon"), [Gravesend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravesend "Gravesend") and [Waterloo Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Bridge "Waterloo Bridge"). These finds hint at the cost involved in making peace with the Vikings. For the next five years, the Danes occupied other parts of England.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrooksGraham-Campbell198691%E2%80%93110-43)

In 876, under Guthrum, Oscetel and Anwend, the Danes slipped past the Saxon army and attacked and occupied [Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham,_Dorset "Wareham, Dorset") in Dorset. Alfred blockaded them but was unable to take Wareham by assault. He negotiated a peace that involved an exchange of hostages and oaths, which the Danes swore on a "holy ring" associated with the worship of [Thor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thor "Thor"). The Danes broke their word, and, after killing all the hostages, slipped away under cover of night to [Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter "Exeter") in Devon.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998148%E2%80%9350-44)

Alfred blockaded the Viking ships in Devon, and with a relief fleet having been scattered by a storm, the Danes were forced to submit. The Danes withdrew to Mercia. In January 878, the Danes made a sudden attack on [Chippenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chippenham "Battle of Chippenham"), a royal stronghold in which Alfred had been staying over Christmas "and most of the people they killed, except the King Alfred, and he with a little band made his way by wood and swamp, and after [Easter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter "Easter") he made a fort at [Athelney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athelney "Athelney") in the marshes of [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset"), and from that fort kept fighting against the foe".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilesIngram1996Year_878-45) Considering the fate of the Mercians' kingdom under similar Viking pressure and an analysis of charter signatories either side of the raid it has been suggested[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2006157-169-46) that Alfred may have fallen prey to a Witan coup at Chippenham rather than simply being surprised by a Viking attack. From his fort at Athelney, an island in the marshes near [North Petherton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Petherton "North Petherton"), Alfred was able to mount a resistance campaign, rallying the local militias from Somerset, [Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiltshire "Wiltshire") and [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39) 878 was the nadir of the history of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. With all the other kingdoms having fallen to the Vikings, Wessex alone was resisting.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988101-47)

### Legend of burnt cake

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legend of burnt cake")]

Having fled to the [Somerset Levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Levels "Somerset Levels"), Alfred was purportedly given shelter by a peasant woman who, unaware of his identity, asked him to mind some wheaten cakes she left baking by the fire.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988101-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2006178-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHorspool20062-49) Preoccupied with the problems of his kingdom, Alfred accidentally let the cakes burn, and was roundly scolded by the woman upon her return. The first written account of the legend appears a century after Alfred's death, though it may have earlier origins in [folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore "Folklore").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHorspool20062-49)

### Counter-attack and victory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Counter-attack and victory")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/King_Alfred%27s_Tower%2C_Stourhead%2C_Somerset.jpg/330px-King_Alfred%27s_Tower%2C_Stourhead%2C_Somerset.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Alfred's_Tower,_Stourhead,_Somerset.jpg)

[King Alfred's Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred's_Tower "King Alfred's Tower") (1772) in [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset"), on the supposed site of Egbert's Stone, the mustering place before the [Battle of Edington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edington "Battle of Edington")[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-51)

In the seventh week after Easter (4–10 May 878), around [Whitsuntide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitsuntide "Whitsuntide"), Alfred rode to [Egbert's Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egbert's_Stone "Egbert's Stone") east of [Selwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selwood,_Somerset "Selwood, Somerset") where he was met by "all the people of Somerset and of [Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiltshire "Wiltshire") and of that part of [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire") which is on this side of the sea (that is, west of [Southampton Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton_Water "Southampton Water")), and they rejoiced to see him".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilesIngram1996Year_878-45) Alfred's emergence from his marshland stronghold was part of a carefully planned offensive that entailed raising the [fyrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrd "Fyrd") of three [shires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire "Shire"). This meant not only that the king had retained the loyalty of [ealdormen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealdormen "Ealdormen"), royal [reeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-reeve "High-reeve") and king's [thegns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thegn "Thegn"), who were charged with levying and leading these forces, but that they had maintained their positions of authority in these localities well enough to answer his summons to war. Alfred's actions also suggest a system of scouts and messengers.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010187%E2%80%93191-52)

Alfred won a decisive victory in the ensuing [Battle of Edington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edington "Battle of Edington") which may have been fought near [Westbury, Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westbury,_Wiltshire "Westbury, Wiltshire"). He then pursued the Danes to their stronghold at [Chippenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chippenham "Chippenham") and starved them into submission. One of the terms of the surrender was that Guthrum convert to Christianity. Three weeks later, the Danish king and 29 of his chief men were baptised at Alfred's court at Aller, near Athelney, with Alfred receiving Guthrum as his spiritual son.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911582%E2%80%93584-39)

According to Asser,

> The unbinding of the [chrisom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrisom "Chrisom")[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-54) on the eighth day took place at a royal estate called [Wedmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedmore "Wedmore").

—Keynes & Lapidge 1983, Ch. 56

At Wedmore, Alfred and Guthrum negotiated what some historians have called the [Treaty of Wedmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Wedmore "Treaty of Wedmore"), but it was to be some years after the cessation of hostilities that a formal treaty was signed.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHorspool2006123%E2%80%93124-55) Under the terms of the so-called Treaty of Wedmore, the converted Guthrum was required to leave Wessex and return to East Anglia. Consequently, in 879 the Viking army left Chippenham and made its way to Cirencester.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge1983Ch._60-56) The formal [Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Alfred_and_Guthrum "Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum"), preserved in [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English") in [Corpus Christi College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi_College,_Cambridge "Corpus Christi College, Cambridge") (Manuscript 383), and in a [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") compilation known as _[Quadripartitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadripartitus "Quadripartitus")_, was negotiated later, perhaps in 879 or 880, when King [Ceolwulf II of Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceolwulf_II_of_Mercia "Ceolwulf II of Mercia") was deposed.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998163-57)

That treaty divided up the kingdom of Mercia. By its terms, the boundary between Alfred's and Guthrum's kingdoms was to run up the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") to the [River Lea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lea "River Lea"), follow the Lea to its source (near [Luton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luton "Luton")), from there extend in a straight line to [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford "Bedford"), and from Bedford follow the [River Ouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Great_Ouse "River Great Ouse") to [Watling Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watling_Street "Watling Street").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAttenborough197498%E2%80%93101[httpsarchiveorgstreamlawsofearliesten00greapage98mode2up_Treaty_of_Alfred_and_Gunthrum]-58)

Alfred succeeded to Ceolwulf's kingdom consisting of western Mercia, and Guthrum incorporated the eastern part of Mercia into an enlarged [Kingdom of East Anglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_East_Anglia "Kingdom of East Anglia") (henceforward known as the [Danelaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danelaw "Danelaw")). By terms of the treaty, moreover, Alfred was to have control over the Mercian city of London and its mints—at least for the time being.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackburn1998105%E2%80%93124-59) In 825, the _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_ had recorded that the people of Essex, Sussex, Kent and Surrey surrendered to [Egbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egbert_of_Wessex "Egbert of Wessex"), Alfred's grandfather. From then until the arrival of the [Great Heathen Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Heathen_Army "Great Heathen Army"), Essex had formed part of Wessex. After the foundation of Danelaw, it appears that some of Essex would have been ceded to the Danes, but how much is not clear.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmyth1995303%E2%80%93304-60)

### 880s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 880s")]

Further information: [Londinium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londinium "Londinium") and [Anglo-Saxon London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_London "Anglo-Saxon London")

With the signing of the [Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Alfred_and_Guthrum "Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum"), an event most commonly held to have taken place around 880 when Guthrum's people began settling [East Anglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Anglia "East Anglia"), Guthrum was neutralised as a threat.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPratt200794-61) The Viking army, which had stayed at Fulham during the winter of 878–79, sailed for Ghent and was active on the continent from 879 to 892.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198386-62)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge1983250%E2%80%93151-63)

There were local raids on the coast of Wessex throughout the 880s. In 882 Alfred fought a small sea battle against four Danish ships. Two of the ships were destroyed, and the others surrendered. This was one of four sea battles recorded in the _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_, three of which involved Alfred.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998171-64) Similar small skirmishes with independent Viking raiders would have occurred for much of the period as they had for decades.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmyth199520%E2%80%9321-65)

In 883 [Pope Marinus I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Marinus_I "Pope Marinus I") exempted the Saxon quarter in Rome from taxation, probably in return for Alfred's promise to send alms annually to Rome, which may be the origin of the medieval tax called [Peter's Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter's_Pence "Peter's Pence"). The pope sent gifts to Alfred, including what was reputed to be a piece of the [True Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_Cross "True Cross").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998190%E2%80%9391-66)

After the signing of the treaty with Guthrum, Alfred was spared any large-scale conflicts for some time. Despite this relative peace, the King was forced to deal with a number of Danish raids and incursions. Among these was a raid in [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), an allied kingdom in [South East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_East_England "South East England"), during the year 885, which was possibly the largest raid since the battles with Guthrum. Asser's account of the raid places the Danish raiders at the Saxon city of [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Kent "Rochester, Kent"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198386-62) where they built a temporary fortress in order to besiege the city. In response to this incursion, Alfred led an [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon "Anglo-Saxon") force against the Danes who, instead of engaging the army of Wessex, fled to their beached ships and sailed to another part of Britain. The retreating Danish force supposedly left Britain the following summer.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198387-67)

Not long after the failed Danish raid in Kent, Alfred dispatched his fleet to East Anglia. The purpose of this expedition is debated, but Asser claims that it was for the sake of plunder.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198387-67) After travelling up the [River Stour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Stour,_Suffolk "River Stour, Suffolk"), the fleet met Danish vessels that numbered 13 or 16 (sources vary on the number), and a battle ensued.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198387-67) The Anglo-Saxon fleet emerged victorious, and as [Henry of Huntingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Huntingdon "Henry of Huntingdon") writes, "laden with spoils".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenry_of_Huntingdon196981-68) The victorious fleet was surprised when attempting to leave the River Stour and was attacked by a Danish force at the mouth of the river. The Danish fleet defeated Alfred's fleet, which may have been weakened in the previous engagement.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodruff199386-69)

### King of the Anglo-Saxons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: King of the Anglo-Saxons")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Southwark_Bridge_City_Plaque.JPG/500px-Southwark_Bridge_City_Plaque.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Southwark_Bridge_City_Plaque.JPG)

A plaque in the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") noting the restoration of the Roman walled city by Alfred

In or shortly before 883, [Æthelred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelred,_Lord_of_the_Mercians "Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians"), the ruler of western Mercia, submitted to Alfred's rule and before 888 married his daughter [Æthelflæd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelfl%C3%A6d "Æthelflæd"). Alfred was now overlord of all Anglo-Saxons not under Danish rule, and in the mid-880s he changed his title from king of the West Saxons to king of the Anglo-Saxons. In 886 Alfred occupied and restored the Mercian town of London and entrusted it to be governed by Æthelred.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998182%E2%80%93186-70) The restoration of London progressed through the latter half of the 880s and probably revolved around a new street plan, adding additional fortifications to the existing Roman walls; and possibly the construction of matching fortifications on the south bank of the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynes199823-71) Guthrum died in 890.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998176-72)

### Viking attacks (890s)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Viking attacks (890s)")]

After another lull, in the autumn of 892 or 893, the Danes attacked again. Finding their position in mainland Europe precarious, they crossed to England in 330 ships in two divisions. They entrenched themselves, the larger body at [Appledore, Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appledore,_Kent "Appledore, Kent"), and the lesser under [Hastein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastein "Hastein"), at [Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton,_Kent "Milton, Kent"), also in Kent. The invaders brought their wives and children with them, indicating a meaningful attempt at conquest and colonisation. Alfred, in 893 or 894, took up a position from which he could observe both forces.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMerkle2009220-73)

While he was in talks with Hastein, the Danes at Appledore broke out and struck north-westwards. They were overtaken by Alfred's eldest son Edward, and were defeated at the [Battle of Farnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Farnham "Battle of Farnham") in Surrey. They took refuge on an island at [Thorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorney,_Buckinghamshire "Thorney, Buckinghamshire"), on the [River Colne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Colne,_Hertfordshire "River Colne, Hertfordshire") between [Buckinghamshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckinghamshire "Buckinghamshire") and [Middlesex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex "Middlesex"), where they were blockaded and forced to give hostages and promise to leave Wessex.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge1983115%E2%80%93116,_286-74)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMerkle2009220-73) They then went to Essex and after suffering another defeat at [Benfleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Benfleet "South Benfleet"), joined with Hastein's force at [Shoebury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoebury "Shoebury").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge1983115%E2%80%93116,_286-74)

Alfred had been on his way to relieve his son at Thorney when he heard that the [Northumbrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria "Northumbria") and East Anglian Danes were besieging [Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter "Exeter") and an unnamed stronghold on the [North Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Devon "North Devon") shore. Alfred at once hurried westward and raised the [Siege of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Exeter_(893)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Siege of Exeter (893) (page does not exist)"). The fate of the other place is not recorded.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911583-75)

The force under Hastein set out to march up the [Thames Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Valley "Thames Valley"), possibly with the idea of assisting their friends in the west. They were met by a large force under the three great ealdormen of [Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia "Mercia"), Wiltshire and Somerset and forced to head off to the north-west, being finally overtaken and blockaded at [Buttington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Buttington "Battle of Buttington"). (Some identify this with Buttington Tump at the mouth of the [River Wye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Wye "River Wye"), others with [Buttington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buttington "Buttington") near [Welshpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welshpool "Welshpool").) An attempt to break through the English lines failed. Those who escaped retreated to Shoebury. After collecting reinforcements, they made a sudden dash across England and occupied the ruined [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") walls of [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester "Chester"). The English did not attempt a winter blockade but contented themselves with destroying all the supplies in the district.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911583-75)

Early in 894 or 895 lack of food obliged the Danes to retire once more to Essex. At the end of the year, the Danes drew their ships up the River Thames and the [River Lea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lea "River Lea") and fortified themselves twenty miles (32 km) north of London. A frontal attack on the Danish lines failed but later in the year, Alfred saw a means of obstructing the river to prevent the egress of the Danish ships. The Danes realised that they were outmanoeuvred, struck off north-westwards and wintered at [Cwatbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quatford "Quatford") near [Bridgnorth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgnorth "Bridgnorth"). The next year, 896 (or 897), they gave up the struggle. Some retired to [Northumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria "Northumbria"), some to East Anglia. Those who had no connections in England returned to the continent.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911583-75)

## Military reorganisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Military reorganisation")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Alfred_the_great_silver_offering_penny_871_899.jpg/250px-Alfred_the_great_silver_offering_penny_871_899.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_the_great_silver_offering_penny_871_899.jpg)

Alfred the Great silver offering penny, 871–99. Legend: AELFRED REX SAXONUM ('Alfred King of the Saxons')

The Germanic tribes who invaded Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries relied upon the unarmoured infantry supplied by their [tribal levy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription"), or [fyrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrd "Fyrd"), and it was upon this system that the military power of the several kingdoms of early Anglo-Saxon England depended.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestonWiseWerner195670-76) The fyrd was a local militia in the Anglo-Saxon shire in which all freemen had to serve; those who refused military service were subject to fines or loss of their land.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHollister196259%E2%80%9360-77) According to the [law code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_law "Anglo-Saxon law") of [King Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex "Ine of Wessex"), issued in c.694:

> If a nobleman who holds land neglects military service, he shall pay 120 shillings and forfeit his land; a nobleman who holds no land shall pay 60 shillings; a commoner shall pay a fine of 30 shillings for neglecting military service

—Attenborough 1974, pp.52–53

Wessex's history of failures preceding Alfred's success in 878 emphasised to him that the traditional system of battle he had inherited played to the Danes' advantage. While the Anglo-Saxons and the Danes attacked settlements for plunder, they employed different tactics. In their raids the Anglo-Saxons traditionally preferred to attack head-on by assembling their forces in a [shield wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shield_wall "Shield wall"), advancing against their target and overcoming the oncoming wall marshalled against them in defence.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998194%E2%80%93195-78) The Danes preferred to choose easy targets, mapping cautious forays to avoid risking their plunder with high-stake attacks for more. Alfred determined their tactic was to launch small attacks from a secure base to which they could retreat should their raiders meet strong resistance.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998194%E2%80%93195-78)

The bases were prepared in advance, often by capturing an estate and augmenting its defences with ditches, [ramparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") and [palisades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palisade "Palisade"). Once inside the fortification, Alfred realised, the Danes enjoyed the advantage, better situated to outlast their opponents or crush them with a counter-attack because the provisions and stamina of the besieging forces waned.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998194%E2%80%93195-78)

The means by which the Anglo-Saxons marshalled forces to defend against marauders also left them vulnerable to the Vikings. It was the responsibility of the shire fyrd to deal with local raids. The king could call up the national militia to defend the kingdom but in the case of the Viking raids, problems with communication and raising supplies meant that the national militia could not be mustered quickly enough. It was only after the raids had begun that a call went out to landowners to gather their men for battle. Large regions could be devastated before the fyrd could assemble and arrive. Although the landowners were obliged to the king to supply these men when called, during the attacks in 878 many of them abandoned their king and collaborated with Guthrum.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2006157%E2%80%93169-79)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998139,_152-80)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon1997398-81)

With these lessons in mind Alfred capitalised on the relatively peaceful years following his victory at Edington with an ambitious restructuring of Saxon defences. On a trip to Rome, Alfred had stayed with Charles the Bald, and it is possible that he may have studied how the Carolingian kings had dealt with Viking raiders. Learning from their experiences he was able to establish a system of taxation and defence for Wessex. There had been a system of fortifications in pre-Viking Mercia that may have been an influence. When the Viking raids resumed in 892 Alfred was better prepared to confront them with a standing, mobile field army, a network of garrisons and a small fleet of ships navigating the rivers and estuaries.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998194-82)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198314-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010212-84)

### Administration and taxation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Administration and taxation")]

Tenants in Anglo-Saxon England had a threefold obligation based on their landholding: the so-called "common burdens" of military service, fortress work, and bridge repair. This threefold obligation has traditionally been called _[trinoda necessitas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinoda\_necessitas "Trinoda necessitas")_ or _trimoda necessitas_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle201070%E2%80%9373-85) The Old English name for the fine due for neglecting military service was _fierdwite_.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAttenborough197452%E2%80%9353-86) To maintain the [burhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burh "Burh"), and to reorganise the fyrd as a standing army, Alfred expanded the tax and conscription system based on the productivity of a tenant's landholding. The hide was the basic unit of the system on which the tenant's public obligations were assessed. A hide is thought to represent the amount of land required to support one family. The hide differed in size according to the value and resources of the land and the landowner would have to provide service based on how many hides he owned.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle201070%E2%80%9373-85)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELapidge2001-87)

### Burghal system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Burghal system")]

See also: [Burghal Hidage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burghal_Hidage "Burghal Hidage")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Anglo-Saxon_burhs.svg/250px-Anglo-Saxon_burhs.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anglo-Saxon_burhs.svg)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Winchesterwalls.jpg/250px-Winchesterwalls.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Winchesterwalls.jpg)

The walled defence round a [burh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burh "Burh"). The [City Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_city_walls "Winchester city walls") of Alfred's capital, [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester"). Saxon and medieval work on Roman foundations.

The foundation of Alfred's new military defence system was a network of burhs, distributed at tactical points throughout the kingdom.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPratt200795-88) There were thirty-three burhs, about 30 kilometres (19 miles) apart, enabling the military to confront attacks anywhere in the kingdom within a day.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHull2006xx-89)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998203-90)

Alfred's burhs (of which 22 developed into [boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough "Borough")) ranged from former [Roman towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Britain "Roman Britain"), such as Winchester, where the stone walls were repaired and ditches added, to massive earthen walls surrounded by wide ditches, probably reinforced with wooden [revetments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revetment "Revetment") and palisades, such as at [Burpham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burpham "Burpham") in West Sussex.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTETait199918-91)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1992127-92)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998304-93)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-95) The size of the burhs ranged from tiny outposts such as [Pilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilton,_Devon "Pilton, Devon") in Devon, to large fortifications in established towns, the largest being at Winchester.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-96)

A document now known as the _[Burghal Hidage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burghal\_Hidage "Burghal Hidage")_ provides an insight into how the system worked. It lists the hidage for each of the fortified towns contained in the document. [Wallingford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallingford,_Oxfordshire "Wallingford, Oxfordshire") had a hidage of 2,400, which meant that the landowners there were responsible for supplying and feeding 2,400 men, the number sufficient for maintaining 9,900 feet (1.88 miles; 3.0 kilometres) of wall.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillRumble19965-97) A total of 27,071 soldiers were needed, approximately one in four of all the free men in Wessex.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998204%E2%80%93207-98) Many of the burhs were twin towns that straddled a river and were connected by a fortified bridge, like those built by Charles the Bald a generation before.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198314-83) The double-burh blocked passage on the river, forcing Viking ships to navigate under a garrisoned bridge lined with men armed with stones, spears or arrows. Other burhs were sited near fortified royal villas, allowing the king better control over his strongholds.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998198%E2%80%93202-99)

The burhs were connected by a road system maintained for army use (known as [herepaths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herepath "Herepath")). The roads allowed an army quickly to be assembled, sometimes from more than one burh, to confront the Viking invader.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle200326-100) The road network posed significant obstacles to Viking invaders, especially those laden with booty. The system threatened Viking routes and communications making it far more dangerous for them. The Vikings lacked the equipment for a siege against a burh and a developed doctrine of [siegecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegecraft "Siegecraft"), having tailored their methods of fighting to rapid strikes and unimpeded retreats to well-defended fortifications. The only means left to them was to starve the burh into submission but this gave the king time to send his field army or garrisons from neighbouring burhs along the army roads. In such cases, the Vikings were extremely vulnerable to pursuit by the king's joint military forces.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1988204,_304-101) Alfred's burh system posed such a formidable challenge against Viking attack that when the Vikings returned in 892 and stormed a half-built, poorly garrisoned fortress up the [Lympne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lympne "Lympne") estuary in Kent, the Anglo-Saxons were able to limit their penetration to the outer frontiers of Wessex and Mercia.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998287,_304-102) Alfred's burghal system was revolutionary in its strategic conception and potentially expensive in its execution. His contemporary biographer Asser wrote that many nobles balked at the demands placed upon them even though they were for "the common needs of the kingdom".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-103)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998206-104)

### English navy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: English navy")]

Alfred also tried his hand at naval design. In 896 he ordered the construction of a small fleet, perhaps a dozen or so longships that, at 60 oars, were twice the size of Viking warships.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988111-105) This was not, as the Victorians asserted, the birth of the [English Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Navy "English Navy").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirthSebo2020329%E2%80%93331-106) Wessex had possessed a royal fleet before this. Alfred's older brother sub-king [Æthelstan of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelstan_of_Kent "Æthelstan of Kent") and Ealdorman Ealhhere had defeated a Viking fleet in 851 capturing nine ships and Alfred had conducted naval actions in 882.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage198886%E2%80%9388,_97-107) The year 897 marked an important development in the naval power of Wessex. The author of the _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_ related that Alfred's ships were larger, swifter, steadier and rode higher in the water than either Danish or [Frisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisians "Frisians") ships. It is probable that, under the classical tutelage of Asser, Alfred used the design of [Greek and Roman warships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic-era_warships "Hellenistic-era warships"), with high sides, designed for fighting rather than for navigation.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-108)

Alfred had seapower in mind; if he could intercept raiding fleets before they landed, he could spare his kingdom from being ravaged. Alfred's ships may have been superior in conception, but in practice they proved to be too large to manoeuvre well in the close waters of estuaries and rivers, the only places in which a naval battle could be fought.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998305%E2%80%93307-109)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirthSebo2020329%E2%80%93331-106) The warships of the time were not designed to be ship killers but rather troop carriers. It has been suggested that, like sea battles in late Viking age Scandinavia, these battles may have entailed a ship coming alongside an opposing vessel, lashing the two ships together and then boarding the craft. The result was a land battle involving hand-to-hand fighting on board the two lashed vessels.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010286%E2%80%93297-110)

In the one recorded naval engagement in 896, Alfred's new fleet of nine ships intercepted six Viking ships at the mouth of an unidentified river in the south of England. The Danes had beached half their ships and gone inland.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilesIngram1996Year_896-111)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988111-105) Alfred's ships immediately moved to block their escape. The three Viking ships afloat attempted to break through the English lines. Only one made it; Alfred's ships intercepted the other two.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988111-105) Lashing the Viking boats to their own, the English crew boarded and proceeded to kill the Vikings. One ship escaped because Alfred's heavy ships became grounded when the tide went out.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010286%E2%80%93297-110) A land battle ensued between the crews. The Danes were heavily outnumbered, but as the tide rose, they returned to their boats which, with shallower drafts, were freed first. The English watched as the Vikings rowed past them but they suffered so many casualties (120 dead against 62 Frisians and English) that they had difficulty putting out to sea.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010286%E2%80%93297-110) All were too damaged to row around Sussex, and two were driven against the Sussex coast (possibly at [Selsey Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selsey_Bill "Selsey Bill")).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988111-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTELavelle2010286%E2%80%93297-110) The shipwrecked crew were brought before Alfred at Winchester and hanged.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTESavage1988111-105)

## Legal reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Legal reform")]

Main article: [Doom book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_book "Doom book")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Alfred_king_of_Wessex_London_880.jpg/250px-Alfred_king_of_Wessex_London_880.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_king_of_Wessex_London_880.jpg)

A coin of Alfred, London, 880 (based upon a Roman model)

In the late 880s or early 890s, Alfred issued a long _[domboc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domboc "Domboc")_ or [law code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_code "Law code") consisting of his own laws, followed by a code issued by his late seventh-century predecessor King [Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex "Ine of Wessex").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAttenborough197462%E2%80%9393-112) Together these laws are arranged into 120 chapters. In his introduction Alfred explains that he gathered together the laws he found in many "[synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod")-books" and "ordered to be written many of the ones that our forefathers observed—those that pleased me; and many of the ones that did not please me, I rejected with the advice of my councillors, and commanded them to be observed in a different way".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-113)

Alfred singled out in particular the laws that he "found in the days of Ine, my kinsman, or [Offa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offa "Offa"), king of the Mercians, or King [Æthelberht of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht_of_Kent "Æthelberht of Kent") who first among the English people received baptism". He appended, rather than integrated, the laws of Ine into his code and although he included, as had Æthelbert, a scale of payments in compensation for injuries to various body parts, the two injury tariffs are not aligned. Offa is not known to have issued a law code, leading historian [Patrick Wormald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Wormald "Patrick Wormald") to speculate that Alfred had in mind the legatine [capitulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitulary "Capitulary") of 786 that was presented to Offa by the [papal legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_legate "Papal legate")[George of Ostia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_of_Ostia "George of Ostia").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2001280%E2%80%93281-114)

About a fifth of the law code is taken up by Alfred's introduction which includes translations into English of the [Ten Commandments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Commandments "Ten Commandments"), a few chapters from the [Book of Exodus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Exodus "Book of Exodus"), and the Apostolic Letter from the [Acts of the Apostles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_the_Apostles "Acts of the Apostles") (15:23–29). The introduction may best be understood as Alfred's meditation upon the meaning of Christian law.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPratt2007215-115) It traces the continuity between God's gift of law to Moses to Alfred's own issuance of law to the West Saxon people. By doing so, it linked the holy past to the historical present and represented Alfred's law-giving as a type of divine legislation.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbels1998248-116)

Similarly Alfred divided his code into 120 chapters because 120 was the age at which Moses died and, in the number-symbolism of early medieval biblical exegetes, 120 stood for law.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2001417-117) The link between [Mosaic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_law "Mosaic law") and Alfred's code is the Apostolic Letter which explained that Christ "had come not to shatter or annul the commandments but to fulfill them; and he taught mercy and meekness" (Intro, 49.1). The mercy that Christ infused into Mosaic law underlies the injury tariffs that figure so prominently in barbarian law codes since Christian synods "established, through that mercy which Christ taught, that for almost every misdeed at the first offence secular lords might with their permission receive without sin the monetary compensation which they then fixed".[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-keynes-118)

The only crime that could not be compensated with a payment of money was treachery to a lord "since Almighty God adjudged none for those who despised Him, nor did Christ, the Son of God, adjudge any for the one who betrayed Him to death; and He commanded everyone to love his lord as Himself".[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-keynes-118) Alfred's transformation of Christ's commandment, from "Love your neighbour as yourself" (Matt. 22:39–40) to love your secular lord as you would love the Lord Christ himself, underscores the importance that Alfred placed upon lordship which he understood as a sacred bond instituted by God for the governance of man.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-119)

When one turns from the _domboc_'s introduction to the laws themselves, it is difficult to uncover any logical arrangement. The impression is of a hodgepodge of miscellaneous laws. The law code, as it has been preserved, is singularly unsuitable for use in lawsuits. In fact, several of Alfred's laws contradicted [the laws of Ine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex#Laws "Ine of Wessex") that form an integral part of the code. Patrick Wormald's explanation is that Alfred's law code should be understood not as a legal manual but as an ideological manifesto of kingship "designed more for symbolic impact than for practical direction".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWormald2001427-120) In practical terms the most important law in the code may well have been the first: "We enjoin, what is most necessary, that each man keep carefully his oath and his pledge" which expresses a fundamental tenet of Anglo-Saxon law.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-121)

Alfred devoted considerable attention and thought to judicial matters. Asser underscores his concern for judicial fairness. Alfred, according to Asser, insisted upon reviewing contested judgments made by his ealdormen and reeves and "would carefully look into nearly all the judgements which were passed [issued] in his absence anywhere in the realm to see whether they were just or unjust".[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-122) A charter from the reign of his son Edward the Elder depicts Alfred as hearing one such appeal in his chamber while washing his hands.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-123)

Asser represents Alfred as a [Solomonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judgement_of_Solomon "Judgement of Solomon") judge, painstaking in his own judicial investigations and critical of royal officials who rendered unjust or unwise judgments. Although Asser never mentions Alfred's law code he does say that Alfred insisted that his judges be literate so that they could apply themselves "to the pursuit of wisdom". The failure to comply with this royal order was to be punished by loss of office.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-124)

The _Anglo-Saxon Chronicle_, commissioned at the time of Alfred, was probably written to promote unification of England,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker200748%E2%80%9350-125) whereas Asser's _The Life of King Alfred_ promoted Alfred's achievements and personal qualities. It was possible that the document was designed this way so that it could be disseminated in Wales because Alfred had acquired overlordship of that country.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker200748%E2%80%9350-125)

## Foreign relations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_the_Great&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Foreign relations")]

Asser speaks grandiosely of Alfred's relations with foreign powers but little definite information is available.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911583-75) His interest in foreign countries is shown by the insertions which he made in his translation of [Orosius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orosius "Orosius"). He corresponded with [Elias III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_III_of_Jerusalem "Elias III of Jerusalem"), the [patriarch of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Patriarch_of_Jerusalem "Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlummer1911583-75) and embassies to Rome conveying the English alms to the pope were fairly frequent.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeynesLapidge198314-83)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-126)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-128) Around 890, [Wulfstan of Hedeby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulfstan_of_Hedeby "Wulfstan of Hedeby") undertook a journey from [Hedeby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedeby "Hedeby") on [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland") along the [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea "Baltic Sea") to the Prussian trading town of [Truso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truso "Truso"). Alfred personally collected details of this trip.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Alfred_the_Great#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrosiusHampson185516-129)
